newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi defence head set for uneasy U.S. talks.
newsitem.headline: Saudi defence head set for uneasy U.S. talks.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's defence minister will carry sensitive political baggage to upcoming Washington talks where a probe into last year's bombing against Americans in the kingdom is expected to be high on the agenda.
Prince Sultan is due to visit Paris on Saturday and continue on to the United States, which he last visited in October 1995, for what diplomats in the kingdom described as "uneasy talks".

Western diplomats and political observers following the relations between Washington and Riyadh expect the talks to cover the Saudi probe into the June truck bombing that killed 19 American soldiers in Dhahran, a potential sale of U.S. fighter jets to Saudi as well as the Middle East peace process.

They said the new administration of President Bill Clinton would likely press Riyadh to share more information on the blast as well as on dissent in the kingdom where Moslem militants have condemned the royal family as subservient to Washington.

"The Americans are a bit in the dark not only over the investigation, but also on the internal politics in Saudi and dissent," said one diplomat. "But the question is how much the Saudis will be willing to give up. They don't believe they need to share information with the Americans or anybody else."
The talks are set against a backdrop of U.S. complaints that the Saudis are not telling Washington enough about the probe.
A senior FBI official last week told Congress the Saudis had given the U.S. the names of people they regarded as suspects in the attack but not the evidence to support their conclusions.
Diplomats speak of "some tension" in ties over the blast, but say the two countries remain strong allies capable of overcoming major differences.

Giving up information on delicate political matters has never been easy for the Saudis and now, with U.S. media allegations that the kingdom has uncovered Iranian involvement in the blast, it will be even harder, they said.
Iran denied the allegations and Saudi Arabia, describing the press reports as unfounded, said only it had the full details and would reveal them when the investigation was completed.
The diplomats said that if Iran's alleged role is confirmed, the Saudi government would be in a tight spot.

A direct accusation of Iran would antagonise the regional non-Arab power. On the other hand blaming Saudi elements would highlight political unrest at home, which the government has always been keen to play down.
"The Saudis are trying to find a convenient formula that will not directly point to Iran and at the same time, will not highlight home-grown dissent," one diplomat said.

"If, for instance, they say that Saudis that were trained in (pro-Iranian) Hizbollah camps (in Lebanon) were behind it, this would be a good face-saving formula. They don't directly blame Iran and they avoid showing internal problems," he added.

They said the United States would only take action against Iran if it had independent confirmation of an Iranian government role. So far U.S. investigators in Saudi Arabia have not been allowed to interview more than 40 detained suspects, they added.
The evidence may point in a convenient direction but the punishment handed down by the Saudi authorities could have serious domestic repercussions, Saudi observers said.
In a stern warning against dissent, four Saudis were beheaded last year after confessing on television to the 1995 bombing that killed five Americans and two Indians in Riyadh.
The executions were preceeded by threats that punishment of the four men would trigger retaliation.
"The Saudi government is worried that more beheadings will only lead to more violence," said a Western diplomat in Riyadh. "They're in a tough position. It could be an eye for an eye."

Prince Sultan is also expected to discuss a possible U.S. deal to sell F-16 fighter aircraft to Saudi Arabia, an issue that has already triggered concern from Israel, also a staunch U.S. ally in the Middle East.
Prince Sultan denied he would clinch a deal in Washington but said the kingdom was looking to replace its tiring fleet of U.S. F-5 fighters adding that the F-16 was a front-runner.
He said his visit would focus on the new administration's strategies in the Middle East and Saudi Arabia.
